backups.name: South Route
hazards: Cornices on the south-ridge catwalk near Point 6125' — multiple failures witnessed; avoid before a solid snow-free window
Loose talus and several rock gendarmes along the summit ridge requiring careful routefinding
Cliff bands just below the ridge crest — stay close to the crest, dropping right (east) only to bypass obstacles
Bushwhacking (blueberry, alder) on off-trail sections above Merritt Lake and on any Mount Howard traverse extension
Rough, pothole/rock-strewn Forest Road 657 access — high-clearance vehicle recommended
backups.overview: Mount Mastiff (6,747 ft) is the third-highest point on Nason Ridge, roughly a mile east of Mount Howard (7,063 ft), overlooking Lake Wenatchee and the US-2 corridor between Leavenworth and Stevens Pass. The South (Southeast Ridge) Route climbs from the Merritt Lake trailhead through old-growth forest to Merritt Lake, then leaves the maintained trail to follow the ridge crest to the broad, flat summit — a Class 2 scramble with one or two Class 3 moves around rock gendarmes, popular as a long day trip and often paired with Mount Howard.
backups.beta: Most parties start from the Merritt Lake Trailhead, hike the maintained trail to Merritt Lake, then follow the Nason Ridge Trail for about a mile and turn uphill on an unsigned boot path that climbs steep forest to Mastiff's southeast ridge (other lines reach the peak from the Crescent Lake basin via the Howard-Mastiff ridge, or up the northeast ridge from Lost Lake). On the ridge, follow the crest -- staying just below it to avoid small cliffs and dense subalpine trees -- to the summit. The route is entirely unmarked past Merritt Lake, so navigation, not climbing difficulty, is the main challenge. Many parties combine the peak with Mount Howard (1 mile west) as a single long day.
backups.turnaround: Because the route is entirely off-trail with no fixed retreat points and afternoon thunderstorms are common on the east-slope Cascades in summer, set a firm turnaround time based on remaining daylight, weather, and party pace before leaving the trailhead, and stick to it even short of the summit.
backups.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; no parking pass or day fee is charged at the Merritt Lake Trailhead.

waypoints.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Signed spur (FR 657) north off Hwy 2 near milepost 76; no permit required, self-register at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 near milepost 76, about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass or 24 miles west of Leavenworth, turn north onto the signed spur for Forest Road 657. The road is rough and high clearance is recommended; drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead at about 3,050 feet. No permit is required, but self-register at the trailhead kiosk before you start hiking.

waypoints.name: Merritt Lake
waypoints.note: Top of the switchbacking Merritt Lake Trail; established campsites and a privy here, and the last dependable water before the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Hike the Merritt Lake Trail as it switchbacks up through forest for about 2.5 miles to Merritt Lake, where there are established campsites, a privy, and the last dependable water before the ridge.

waypoints.name: Boot path split for Mastiff
waypoints.note: About a mile north on the Nason Ridge Trail past the Merritt Lake junction, an unsigned boot path breaks off uphill toward Mastiff's south slopes — easy to walk past if you're not watching for it.
waypoints.directions: Continue past the lake junction onto the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it north about a mile, watching for an unsigned boot path breaking off uphill toward the peak's south slopes. There is no cairn, post or blaze; if the trail starts losing height toward Lost Lake, you have passed the turn and should come back.

waypoints.name: South-slope heather/talus
waypoints.note: Above treeline the boot path fades into open heather and loose talus with no maintained tread and no water; fog or whiteout makes relocating the descent path difficult.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path steeply uphill through forest. Above treeline it fades into open heather and loose talus with no maintained tread and no water, so note landmarks for the descent, especially in fog.

waypoints.name: Mount Mastiff summit
waypoints.note: True summit, third-highest point on Nason Ridge; open views north to Lake Wenatchee and west along the connecting ridge/saddle to Mount Howard, a common combined objective.
waypoints.directions: Gain the ridge and climb it until it turns into a rocky, jagged crest. Follow the moat between rock and snow just to the left, stepping up onto the rock to cross ledges, wrap the big rock tower on its right side close to its base, then scramble dirt and ledges to a knoll and a final snowfield. The summit is broad and flat; the register sits off to the south of the flat area rather than on the high point.

sectionBreakdown.note: A single long day: hike the Merritt Lake trail through second-growth forest and past the lake, then take the Nason Ridge Trail briefly and a boot path up steep forest to the southeast ridge before …

what_to_bring: Trekking poles for talus and the switchbacked approach trail
Map/compass or GPS track for the unmarked boot path above Merritt Lake
Ice axe if snow or cornices linger on the south ridge before August
3+ liters of water — no reliable water source past Merritt Lake
pro_tips: A helmet is recommended for the final ~200 ft of talus/boulder scrambling below the summit
Combine with Mount Howard for a longer Nason Ridge traverse (~13 mi, 5,400+ ft) if doing both peaks in a loop
Self-register at the trailhead kiosk — no Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is currently charged at Merritt Lake Trailhead
watch_out: The boot path above Merritt Lake is faint and easy to lose in trees — carry a map or GPS track
South-ridge cornices can persist into July in heavy-snow years
The last ~200 ft below the summit is loose boulder/talus scrambling
backups.pro_needs: None -- this is a non-technical talus/scree/ridge scramble with no fixed protection or belaying involved on the standard line.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through September. Nason Ridge holds snow and cornices well into early summer; the south ridge's catwalk near Point 6125' is typically corniced into early season and has produced witnessed cornice failures, so waiting for a snow-free window is strongly preferred for the standard non-technical scramble.
backups.approach: From US-2 near milepost 76 (about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass / 24 miles west of Leavenworth), turn onto Forest Road 657 (rough, high-clearance recommended) and drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,050 ft). Hike the Merritt Lake Trail up toward the ridge, connecting with the Nason Ridge Trail; figure a long day (roughly 10 miles round trip, ~4,900 ft gain for Mastiff alone) or an overnight via Merritt or Lost Lake.
backups.descent_text: Descend by the same southeast-ridge line, staying close to the ridge crest and again favoring the east side to reverse the gendarme bypass near 6,125 ft (loose rock and talus underfoot - go slow, this is the section most prone to kicking rocks onto anyone below). Where the boot path leaves the crest, follow it down through the forest to the Nason Ridge Trail, walk back about a mile to the Merritt Lake junction, and take the maintained Merritt Lake Trail down to the trailhead. This is entirely a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved anywhere on this route; the terrain throughout is Class 2-3 scrambling on talus, scree, and broken rock. The only real descent hazards are loose rock (helmet recommended, especially in groups), the boot path off the ridge fading into open heather and talus with no maintained tread - fog or flat late-day light makes it genuinely hard to relocate - and the fact that the route should not be down-climbed wet or icy since the rock gets slick.
backups.bail: There are no fixed rappel stations or established bail points; retreat is by reversing the ascent ridge/scree line back toward Merritt Lake. In poor visibility, or on corniced/snow-covered ridge sections (common into early summer), descend off the ridge crest onto the south-facing scree rather than risk the steep, cliffy east side of the peak.

itinerary.cal: Lower slopes are south/east-facing and melt out early, but patchy snow above ~4,400 ft can persist into June-July, so an ice axe/microspikes are worth carrying for early-season attempts.

days.note: A single long day: hike the Merritt Lake trail through second-growth forest and past the lake, then follow the Nason Ridge Trail briefly and a boot path up steep forest and open heather to the southeast ridge before a short class 2-3 scramble along the crest to the summit. Return the same way. Expect lingering snow on the upper slopes into early summer, which slows travel and can require an axe/microspikes.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: Start on the Merritt Lake trail; earlier starts are common in summer to beat heat and afternoon thunderstorms.

schedule.label: Reach Merritt Lake
schedule.detail: About 2.5 mi and ~2,000 ft of the day's gain to the lake basin.

schedule.label: Leave the ridge trail and gain the southeast ridge
schedule.detail: Climb the boot path through forest, heather and talus to the southeast ridge; snow patches common through June.

schedule.label: Summit Mount Mastiff
schedule.detail: Short class 2-3 scramble along the ridge crest to the 6,747 ft summit.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent route down the ridge, the boot path and past Merritt Lake.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Typical car-to-car time for a fit party is 8-9 hours; parties combining Mastiff with neighboring Mount Howard often take 12-14 hours.

days.objective: Summit Mount Mastiff via Merritt Lake and the southeast ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A single, long car-to-car scramble day: roughly 8-9 hours, 10 miles, and 4,900 ft of gain - no camp is used on the standard South Route.

access.passRequired: No fee currently required at Merritt Lake Trailhead (self-register; no toilet or water on site) — confirm before visiting since fee requirements can change.

overnight_permit.where: Nason Ridge is national forest land outside any wilderness; a recreation pass may be needed at the trailheads.

road.name: US-2 (MP 76) via Forest Road 657 to Merritt Lake Trailhead
road.driveNote: Turn off US-2 at milepost 76 (~11.5 mi east of Stevens Pass, ~24 mi west of Leavenworth) onto Forest Road 657, a rough dirt road; follow it 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. High-clearance/AWD recommended when wet.

climate.typical: Summer days on the exposed ridge are warm, sometimes over 80°F with little shade above Merritt Lake; snow and cornices can linger on the north-facing south-ridge catwalk into July.

bySeason.fall: Cools quickly by late September/October; early snow possible above about 5,500 ft.
bySeason.spring: Snow-covered above Merritt Lake into June; active cornices on the south ridge — check NWAC before any spring attempt.
bySeason.summer: Best window (mid-July through September); generally dry and warm with occasional afternoon thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: Becomes a ski/snowshoe approach toward Merritt and Lost Lakes; the summit ridge is avalanche/cornice terrain and not a standard winter scramble objective.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone (winter/spring avalanche/cornice conditions); NWS Wenatchee Mountains zone for summer weather

emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Leavenworth (this office absorbed the former Lake Wenatchee Ranger District)

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in August during the optimal dry window; combined Mastiff+Howard club scrambles add occasional group traffic
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low-moderate - roughly a few dozen parties per summer; mostly Mountaineers club scramble outings, trip-report regulars, and Nason Ridge peak-baggers rather than casual hikers

fitnessSpec.hiking: ~10 miles round trip with roughly 4,900 ft of gain via the Nason Ridge trail and meadows; a long full day on the ridge
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Standard day-scramble pack (~15-20 lb: water, layers, navigation, basic first aid) - no technical rack needed for this route

partner_requirements.approachTime: ~5 hours to the summit from the Merritt Lake trailhead (per on-the-ground trip reports), longer if combined with Mount Howard
requiredSkills: off-trail routefinding through heather and talus (trail thins above treeline)
steady footing on loose scree and steep heather slopes
basic exposure tolerance for narrow ridge sections
map/GPS navigation - route is not signed or continuously trailed
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler - comfortable with off-trail routefinding, loose talus, and short exposed Class 3 ridge moves; not a beginner hike despite the Class 2-3 grade

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September, with August the clear high point

July.reason: Lingering snow patches on upper slopes and in the basin below the ridge into early-mid July; becomes good once melted out by late July

August.reason: Driest, most stable conditions; slopes fully melted out - the best window with dry heather/talus

September.reason: Still dry and clear typically, but shorter daylight and higher chance of an early-season cold snap or first snowfall late in the month

weather.typical: Transitional east-Cascades climate, drier than the crest - clear and stable most of the optimal window
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are possible on the exposed ridge in August, consistent with typical Cascades summer convective patterns

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Class 2-3 terrain with loose scree, steep heather, and a long day on an open ridge; short exposed scrambling moves on the narrow, rocky, craggy sections of the ridge mean a slip could result in a serious fall, though it is not sustained high-angle exposure

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; the nearest NWAC coverage is the Stevens Pass zone, which is only relevant to spring/winter travel here, not this route's July-September climbing window

gaps: First-ascent history not documented in available sources

Mileage/gain figures vary modestly by source (10 mi/3,330 ft per WTA & Mountaineers vs. ~11 mi/5,000 ft in a combined ski-route trip report covering extra terrain) — figures used here are for the standard summer scramble
GPS track sourced from public CalTopo map: https://caltopo.com/m/3011N

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From US-2 near milepost 76 (about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass / 24 miles west of Leavenworth), turn onto Forest Road 657 (rough, high-clearance recommended) and drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,050 ft).

backups.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble with talus, bushwhacking, and gendarmes on the ridge. Trip reports cite helmets and ice axes; rope not part of standard gear list.
backups.corrections: None; Mountaineers.org trip reports confirm scramble-grade terrain with gendarme routefinding, no roped climbing mentioned.

approach_variants.name: Merritt Lake Trail and Nason Ridge Trail
approach_variants.notes: From the highway, turn north onto the signed spur for the rough forest road — high clearance is recommended — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Self-register at the kiosk. The maintained trail switchbacks up through old-growth forest to Merritt Lake, which has established campsites and a privy and is the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue past the lake junction onto the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it north; the unsigned climbers' path toward the peak's south slopes breaks off uphill about a mile along. Above treeline the path fades into open heather and loose talus with no maintained tread and no water at all, and the ridge crest becomes the only handrail to the broad flat summit.
approach_variants.season: July into October once the ridge melts out; commonly done as a long day and often paired with the neighbouring summit a mile west.
hazards: The route is entirely unmarked past Merritt Lake — navigation, not climbing difficulty, is the main challenge
Open heather and loose talus above treeline with no tread
Fog or whiteout makes relocating the descent path genuinely difficult
No water above Merritt Lake
One or two Class 3 moves around rock gendarmes on the crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: Nothing marks the turn — the tell is what happens if you carry straight on. Past Merritt Lake the maintained trail climbs to the ridge trail; a short way along it an unsigned junction sends the climbers' path uphill toward this peak's south slopes. There is no cairn, no post and no blaze, and parties carrying a track have still needed to hunt for it. The overshoot tell is the useful part: going straight on at that junction descends toward Lost Lake, so losing height toward water means you are past the turn and should come back. Higher, the route gives you the one genuinely visual landmark on the mountain — climb the ridge until the snow gives way to a rocky, jagged, narrow crest, which looks impassable at first glance. The line follows the moat between rock and snow just off to the left, stepping up onto the rock to cross ledges, then wraps a big rock tower on its right side, staying close in at its base, and scrambles dirt and ledges to a knoll and one last snowfield. The summit above is bare and flat rather than a point, and the register does not sit on the high point but off to the south of the flat area.

bivy.name: Merritt Lake
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable all season, and the pivot of the whole ridge's water problem: it is the first water eastbound on a bone-dry trail and there is none whatsoever east of it. Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
bivy.capacity: A large, well-established camp with a privy — the only toilet anywhere on this ridge — and room for a number of parties. It is the busiest overnight spot on Nason Ridge and gets weekend traffic from hikers who have no interest in the summits at all.

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

backups.name: Standard Scramble
backups.fa: 1925 - first ascent by a Mountaineers party (reportedly eight climbers) led by Glen Bremerman and C. A. Fisher
hazards: Loose, rotten rock on both the northeast-ridge and South Chimney lines — described in trip reports as generously rated 'Class 3'
Class 5 knife-edge ridge directly connecting the Middle and East (true) summits — most parties must detour via a ledge traverse to avoid it
Persistent snow ramp on the southeast approach (roughly 4,750-5,200 ft) that can linger into July and requires care or an ice axe
River crossings (Kachess River at the trailhead, Mineral Creek below the peak) that are harder and more dangerous during high spring/early-summer flow
backups.overview: Three Queens is a triple-summited peak on Chikamin Ridge in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, the second-highest point on the ridge after Chikamin Peak (6,994 ft). The East Peak (6,693 ft) is the true summit; the Middle (~6,600 ft) and West (~6,400 ft) peaks are linked to it by a narrow, exposed connecting ridge that includes a Class 5 knife-edge section most parties avoid via a ledge traverse. The mountain sits almost directly north of Little Kachess Lake, between Mineral Creek (south/southwest) and the Cooper River (north/east). First climbed in 1925 by a Mountaineers party led by Glen Bremerman and C.A. Fisher; the name was adopted by the USBGN in 1940. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the peak's west slope en route between Spectacle Lake and Chikamin Ridge, though the summit scramble itself leaves the PCT/approach trail well below treeline.
backups.beta: From the Mineral Creek Trail, leave the tread west of the broad waterfall gully and climb off-trail through vine maple and then long south-side talus and scree to the southeast shoulder (about 6,200 ft). From the shoulder, traverse roughly a quarter mile of steep snow or talus onto the northeast ridge, then scramble the final ~400 ft up the ridge to the East (true) summit. The step onto the ridge and the upper ridge are loose, exposed class 3 with a short class 4 move or two, so test every hold. A separate, longer line from a camp at Upper Park Lake climbs the north side to the Main-Middle notch and crosses a ledge system on the north face; it is a different route, not part of this one.
backups.turnaround: Turn around if snow is hard without an axe or weather builds.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
backups.descent: Reverse the scramble toward the approach basin.
obj_haz: loose talus and scree on the summit approach slopes
exposed, loose rock on the northeast-ridge finish
unbridged Kachess River ford near the trailhead

waypoints.name: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331)
waypoints.note: Signed trailhead at the bottom of the valley on FR 4600, ~3 mi past Cooper Pass; self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, no fee.
waypoints.directions: Drive FR-4600 over Cooper Pass and stay on it about 3 miles past the pass, down to the signed Mineral Creek Trailhead on the valley floor at roughly 2,360-2,400 ft. There is a self-issue wilderness permit kiosk at the trailhead and no fee, so fill one out before you start. Trail #1331 leaves the parking area and crosses the Kachess River almost immediately — look for logs spanning it, and expect a short, easy wade when they are not in place.

waypoints.name: Kachess River crossing
waypoints.note: Ford or rock-hop the Kachess River right at the start of the trail; can run thigh-deep in early-season high water.

waypoints.name: Old mine / end of mining-road tread
waypoints.note: Trail follows an old mining road through old-growth forest to this point, then narrows just before the wilderness boundary.

waypoints.name: Mineral Creek log crossing
waypoints.note: Cross Mineral Creek on a skinny, wet log (a crisscrossed pair aids balance); slick and exposed enough that some parties build/adjust a log bridge here.

waypoints.name: Leave Mineral Creek Trail for brush/gully ascent
waypoints.note: About a mile past the creek crossing, below the Three Queens massif, leave the maintained trail and start climbing brush and gully terrain toward open talus.

waypoints.name: Talus slope to the southeast shoulder
waypoints.note: Open talus that steepens and turns smaller and looser higher up leads to the broad southeast shoulder; loose underfoot.

waypoints.name: Traverse onto the northeast ridge
waypoints.note: Cross about a quarter mile of steep snow or talus from the shoulder to the northeast ridge; the step onto the ridge is the loosest, most exposed move of the day.

waypoints.name: Three Queens summit
waypoints.note: True summit, reached by the final loose, exposed stretch of the northeast ridge; test every hold.

sectionBreakdown.note: A long single-day scramble up the Mineral Creek Trail, then off-trail up talus/snow to the southeast shoulder and a traverse onto the northeast ridge for a sust…

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful early season for snow in the approach basins.
what_to_bring: Helmet (loose rock is the dominant hazard on every line)
Trekking poles for the river fords
Ice axe if snow remains on the southeast-approach snow ramp (common into July)
Light rope and a few pieces of gear if planning the South Chimney (Class 4) variant, plus rap rings/webbing for the two ~60 ft rappels
pro_tips: Identify the true (highest) of the three summits
Snow lingers in the basins into July
watch_out: Do not commit to the direct Middle-to-East summit ridge — back off and take the ledge traverse below it instead
Test rock carefully before weight-bearing on the upper northeast ridge and South Chimney; rockfall risk to parties below
Log crossings over Mineral Creek/Kachess River can be slick; have a wading backup plan
backups.best_season: Late July through September is most reliable — the southeast-approach snow ramp (~4,750-5,200 ft) commonly persists into July, and the loose rock on both standard lines is safest to negotiate once fully snow-free; FR 4600 access itself is often not open until early-mid summer.
backups.approach: Trailhead: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331), roughly 2,360-2,400 ft, reached via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass. From the parking area the trail promptly crosses the Kachess River — look for logs spanning it; when they're not in place it's a short, easy wade. The trail then climbs gently north through second-growth and brushy old avalanche paths, muddy in spots with the occasional blowdown to step over. At about 1.6-1.7 miles it crosses Mineral Creek itself; this crossing carries enough current in early season that parties often lay a short log/rock crossing rather than ford, and the ruins of an old mine and mill sit just off-trail here as a landmark (and a fine last water source). Continue upstream through brushy trail for roughly another mile, to about the 2.7-mile mark, watching on the right (west) for a break in the timber around 3,300-3,500 ft — this is where an obvious boot/social path leaves the maintained trail and cuts west through 100-200 ft of vine-maple brush to reach the base of Three Queens' south-face talus. Leave the trail west of the broad waterfall gully that drains the south face (not the drainage directly above the creek crossing) — trip reports flag this junction as easy to get wrong in the brush. From here it's off-trail talus and scree for the remaining 1,400-1,700 ft of gain: the lower ~1,000 ft is moderately angled, largely stable large talus; above that the rock turns smaller and looser, funneling into choss gullies that run generally class 2 with short class 3 sections higher up. A snow ramp (commonly encountered around 5,200 ft) can persist into midsummer on some lines, so carry an ice axe for early-season attempts. Loose rock and rockfall are the dominant hazards through the upper talus and gullies — wear a helmet and keep the group tight so climbers aren't stacked below one another. The final ~400 ft to the 6,693-ft high point is the most exposed scrambling on the route, with brief but genuine class 3 moves and blocks that can shift underfoot; published descriptions of this section as 'class 3' are considered generous by several parties who found it heads-up the whole way.
backups.descent_text: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: back down the summit scrambling, through the upper choss gullies, down the talus to the vine-maple break, and out the 2.7-2.8 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek Trailhead. No rappelling is required on this walk-off/downclimb line (rappels: 0), but the loose upper talus and gullies are generally regarded as more hazardous descending than climbing — face in through the class 3 sections, move deliberately on the small unstable talus, and regroup below rockfall lines rather than descending stacked up. Any snow ramp encountered on the ascent is often the fastest way down (plunge-step or glissade with an axe). Total time from summit to car is commonly reported around 3.5-4 hours. Note: if a party instead climbs the optional South Chimney variant (class 4, on the south face) rather than the standard talus/gully line, that route does NOT walk off — the chimney itself is descended by rappel: two rappels of about 60 ft each, reported consistently in trip logs. Anchors are natural (chockstones, horns, or slung blocks), as this is unbolted alpine rock, so carry cord/webbing to build or back up anchors. A single 60m rope handles both rappels doubled; two shorter ropes joined also work. Below the chimney, the descent rejoins the same long talus and scree slopes and the trail out. Hazards specific to this variant are loose rock in the chimney and rope-snag risk against the blocky walls.

pitch_detail.notes: Long, steepening talus and scree slope off-trail from the Mineral Creek Trail up the south side to the southeast shoulder
pitch_detail.pitch: Talus/scree ascent to the southeast shoulder

pitch_detail.notes: Traverse about a quarter mile from the southeast shoulder onto the northeast ridge (steep snow early season), then roughly 400 ft of loose, exposed ridge scrambling to the East summit
pitch_detail.pitch: Shoulder traverse and northeast ridge to summit

itinerary.cal: Snow can linger on the shoulder traverse into July, so carry an ice axe (and consider microspikes) for early-season attempts.

days.note: A long single-day scramble up the Mineral Creek Trail, then off-trail up talus/snow to the southeast shoulder and a traverse onto the northeast ridge for a sustained, loose class-3 finish. No camping — parties are back at the trailhead by afternoon/early evening.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble to East Peak

schedule.label: Leave Mineral Creek Trailhead (2,360 ft)
schedule.detail: Ford the Kachess River right at the start; trail runs through old clearcuts and second growth.

schedule.label: Cross Mineral Creek
schedule.detail: Brushy tread for the first few miles before it settles into forest.

schedule.label: Leave the trail into the basin below the shoulder
schedule.detail: Begin the off-trail talus and (early season) snow climb toward Chikamin Ridge.

schedule.label: Gain the southeast shoulder (~6,200 ft)
schedule.detail: Traverse roughly 0.25 mile of steep snow/talus over to the northeast ridge.

schedule.label: Summit East Peak (6,693 ft)
schedule.detail: Loose class-3 scrambling near the top with real exposure; test every hold before weighting it.

schedule.label: Back at the trailhead

days.objective: Summit East Peak (6,693 ft) via the southeast shoulder and northeast ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day: about 10 miles round trip and 4,600 ft of gain, roughly 9-10 hours car-to-car (about 5 hrs up, 3.5-4 hrs down) — no overnight camp is involved.

access.fees: $5 daily or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass; no separate climbing fee
access.rules: Alpine Lakes Wilderness rules apply: no bikes or wheeled vehicles beyond the trailhead, group size limited to 12 (people plus stock combined), practice Leave No Trace, and campfires are restricted in some nearby basins (e.g., Park Lakes)
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead (fill out on entry)
access.closures: Three Queens Fire area closure (order 06-17-03-2026-44): Mineral Creek Trail 1331 is closed through October 31, 2026 unless the order is rescinded sooner. Otherwise FR 4600 is typically snow-closed into early summer, and the trailhead ford of the Kachess River can be hazardous during high spring runoff.

road.name: Cooper Lake Road / Forest Road 4600 (FR 46)
road.status: Gravel forest road, generally passable to passenger cars in dry conditions; washboard and potholes reported near Cooper Pass
road.driveNote: About 9-10 miles on FR 4600 from the Salmon La Sac Rd junction, over Cooper Pass, down to the signed trailhead at the valley bottom
road.seasonalGate: Snowed in / gated at lower elevations through winter and spring; typically not reliably open until early-mid summer — check the Cle Elum Ranger District road report before driving

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with heavy orographic precipitation, especially as winter snowfall; the Alpine Lakes high country typically holds snow into early summer.

bySeason.fall: Good, cooler conditions through September; watch for early snow at elevation and shortening daylight
bySeason.spring: Trailhead access blocked by snow on FR 4600 into May/June most years; high river flows make the Kachess River ford hazardous
bySeason.summer: Prime window; a snow ramp on the southeast approach commonly lingers into July, so the route is easiest and most reliably Class 3 from mid/late July on
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — road access is typically snowed in and the route becomes a serious mixed/avalanche-prone undertaking

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to absent along FR 4600 and on the mountain; the nearest reliable help is the Cle Elum area
emergency.rangerStation: Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, 803 W 2nd St, Cle Elum, WA 98922 — (509) 852-1100
emergency.nearestHospital: Kittitas Valley Healthcare, 603 S Chestnut St, Ellensburg, WA — full 24-hour ER (roughly 50 miles / ~1 hour drive from the trailhead via Salmon La Sac Rd and I-90); Kittitas Valley Healthcare also runs an urgent-care-only clinic in Cle Elum, closer but not a full ER
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Kittitas County Sheriff's Office — 911 for emergencies, (509) 925-8534 non-emergency

crowds.peakTraffic: No sharp peak; scattered visits July-September, skewed toward summer weekends when scramble clubs (e.g. The Mountaineers) run trips to the area
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - no hard count found, but sparse trip-report history (a handful of documented trips per year) suggests roughly 10-25 parties per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long single-day approach on the Mineral Creek trail, followed by off-trail talus/slope travel to the true (east) summit; several thousand feet of cumulative gain, so long-day alpine fitness is required
fitnessSpec.packWeight: ~15-20 lb day pack (10 essentials, food, water, layers) if done car-to-car; ~30-35 lb if backpacking in for an overnight base camp

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - about 5 hours up from the Mineral Creek trailhead and 3.5-4 hours down; normally done car-to-car in one day
requiredSkills: off-trail route-finding between the three summits (unmarked, uncairned)
basic snow-travel competence for lingering early-season snow in the approach basins
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler comfortable with unmaintained-trail and off-trail travel; prior scrambling/mountaineering experience is recommended given the route-finding required between the three summits and the loose talus underfoot

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September (July-September); late July still carries some early-season snow risk in the basins

July.reason: Early in the month, snow can still linger in the approach basins and on talus slopes; conditions firm up and improve as the month progresses

August.reason: Most reliably dry and stable window - talus is snow-free, days are longest, and route-finding between summits is easiest

September.reason: Generally stable and dry, but shorter days and the risk of early autumn snow returning to the peak, especially late in the month

weather.typical: Typical central-Cascades summer alpine pattern: clear, cool mornings warming through the day; nights can be cold at ~6,700 ft even in summer; some snow can linger into July in the shaded approach basins
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/showers are an occasional risk in the Central Cascades in July-August; check the NWAC mountain weather forecast for the Snoqualmie Pass zone before a long talus/summit day

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Summit exposure is minor; the primary hazards are loose rock/talus underfoot and route-finding between the three summits rather than sustained exposure. A slip on talus could cause injury, but the terrain is not highly exposed compared to technical alpine routes.

gaps: No confirmed roped/technical grade (e.g., YDS 5th-class rating) for the South Chimney beyond a generic 'Class 4' description in a single trip report
Exact first-ascent route line is not documented, only that the 1925 Mountaineers ascent reached the peak
No official current trail-condition or road-status source consulted beyond secondary trip reports; verify FR 4600 and Mineral Creek Trail status with Cle Elum Ranger District before a trip

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Trailhead: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331), roughly 2,360-2,400 ft, reached via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass.

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek Trail to the break in the timber west of the waterfall gully
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at roughly 2,360 to 2,400 ft via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass, the trail promptly crosses the Kachess River — look for logs, and wade if they are not there. It climbs gently north through second growth and brushy old avalanche paths, muddy in places with occasional blowdown.

At about 1.6 to 1.7 miles it crosses Mineral Creek itself, which carries enough current in early season that parties often lay a log rather than ford. The ruins of an old mine and mill sit just off-trail here — a landmark and the last good water.

Continue upstream through brushy trail roughly another mile, to about the 2.7-mile mark.

About 8.85 km, with 1,400 to 1,700 ft of off-trail gain above the trail.
hazards: An unbridged Kachess River crossing at the trailhead and a Mineral Creek crossing with real current in early season
A brushy, easy-to-miss trail departure between two similar drainages
Loose rock and rockfall through the upper talus and choss gullies — helmets, and keep the group tight
A snow ramp around 5,200 ft persisting into midsummer
Brief but genuine class 3 with shifting blocks on the final 400 ft, harder than the published grade suggests
approach_variants.baseFinding: The takeoff is a break in the timber on the right, and the way to get it right is to know which drainage it is not. At about 2.7 miles, between roughly 3,300 and 3,500 ft, watch on the right (west) for a break in the timber where an obvious boot and social path leaves the maintained trail and cuts west through 100 to 200 ft of vine maple brush to the base of the south-face talus. The discriminator: leave the trail west of the broad waterfall gully that drains the south face — not at the drainage directly above the Mineral Creek crossing. Trip reports flag exactly this junction as easy to get wrong in the brush, and the two drainages are the reason. Old mine ruins at the creek crossing, then roughly another mile, then the break past the waterfall gully. What the ground should do once you are off trail, in order, so you can check yourself without seeing the peak: the lower 1,000 ft is moderately angled, largely stable large talus. Above that the rock turns smaller and looser and funnels into choss gullies, class 2 with short class 3 steps. A snow ramp is commonly met around 5,200 ft and can persist into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season. The final 400 ft is the most exposed ground on the route, with brief but genuine class 3 and blocks that shift underfoot. Published descriptions calling this section class 3 are considered generous by parties who found it heads-up throughout. Not to be confused with the Park Lakes line: a longer two-day route from a camp at Upper Park Lake climbs the north side to the Main-Middle notch and crosses a ledge system on the north face. It is a separate route on the other side of the mountain, and none of the markers above appear on it.

climbing_route.label: Lower south-face talus
climbing_route.notes: From the base of Three Queens' south-face talus it is off-trail talus and scree for the remaining 1,400-1,700 ft of gain; the lower ~1,000 ft is moderately angled, largely stable large talus.

climbing_route.label: Upper choss gullies
climbing_route.notes: Above the lower talus the rock turns smaller and looser, funneling into choss gullies that run generally class 2 with short class 3 sections higher up. A snow ramp (commonly encountered around 5,200 ft) can persist into midsummer on some lines, so carry an ice axe for early-season attempts. Loose rock and rockfall are the dominant hazards through the upper talus and gullies — wear a helmet and keep the group tight so climbers aren't stacked below one another.

climbing_route.label: Final 400 ft to the high point
climbing_route.notes: The final ~400 ft to the 6,693-ft high point is the most exposed scrambling on the route, with brief but genuine class 3 moves and blocks that can shift underfoot; published descriptions of this section as 'class 3' are considered generous by several parties who found it heads-up the whole way.

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin
bivy.notes: The base for Three Queens, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
bivy.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. Campfires are prohibited in Park Lakes Basin specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

backups.name: Southwest Buttress
gear: single rack of cams to #3 Camalot (a #3 is rarely placed)
glacier travel and crevasse rescue kit
ice axe and crampons for the approach gully
60m rope for a double-rope rappel off the summit
hazards: steep, often snow-filled approach gully (to about 35°)
exposed knife-edge summit ridge
crevasses on the Eldorado/Inspiration/McAllister Glaciers en route
backups.overview: The Southwest Buttress is Dorado Needle's longest and most sustained rock route: over 1,000 ft (9 pitches) of quality granite up steep cracks and slabs, past photogenic gendarmes, to an airy knife-edge summit ridge. Rated Grade III, 5.8, it's a popular objective in its own right, reached via the same Eldorado-area glacier approach used for Eldorado Peak and the East Ridge.
backups.beta: A 9-pitch, III, 5.8 alpine rock route established around 1985, rising in a continuous, blocky, bent line from the small glacier shared with Early Morning Spire to the summit, reached via a long glaciated approach from the Eldorado trailhead.
backups.turnaround: Given the length (9-13 pitches) and afternoon-thunderstorm-prone terrain, set an early turnaround time and account for the moat crossing at the base, which becomes more dangerous as the season progresses.
backups.rappels: One double-rope rappel from a fixed ring and sling on the boulder about 10 m north of the summit to the snow below; or one single-rope rappel from the top of the approach gully
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Eldorado/Marble Creek glaciated cirque; carry a satellite communicator.
backups.descent: Either rappel down the approach gully (single rope), or from a large boulder about 10m north of the true summit — which has a fixed rappel ring and sling — make one double-rope rappel.
obj_haz: Moat crossing at the base (roped crossing recommended)

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Same start as the East Ridge; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at about road mile 20, elevation roughly 2,100 ft, and park in the trailhead lot. The climb starts by leaving the parking area and backtracking a short way downstream to find a log or a ford across the Cascade River, then picking up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek. This is the same start the East Ridge uses; the trailhead-to-glacier approach is identical for both.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Open-basin camp option after the first two talus fields and a waterfall crossing.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on the flat glacier shelf used to stage the Inspiration/McAllister glacier traverse.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Cross north across Inspiration Glacier to this col, then drop northwest onto the McAllister Glacier.
waypoints.directions: From high camp, rope up and cross north over the Inspiration Glacier to the col at about 8,000 ft where it meets the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: McAllister Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Descend the McAllister Glacier toward its southwest gap; navigate visible crevasses, especially late-season.
waypoints.directions: From the col, drop northwest onto the McAllister Glacier and descend toward its southwest gap, threading the visible crevasses, which open up late in the season.

waypoints.name: Marble Creek–McAllister pass
waypoints.note: Lowest gap on the SW side of the glacier; cross to the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.
waypoints.directions: Continue across the McAllister to the Marble Creek-McAllister pass, the lowest gap on the southwest side of the glacier, and cross onto the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.

waypoints.name: Base of Southwest Buttress gully
waypoints.note: A snow-filled gully roughly 700 vertical feet below the pass leads to the start of the buttress climbing.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: 9-pitch, Grade III, 5.7-5.8 buttress tops out on the true summit after a left-leaning corner on the upper ridge.

sectionBreakdown.note: Same Eldorado Creek trail approach, continuing over talus and the Eldorado Glacier toward the Inspiration/McAllister Glacier area, camping within striking distance of the snow gull…
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Approach to high camp near the McAllister/Marble Creek col

sectionBreakdown.note: Cross the glacier to the snow-filled gully below the col, gain the blocky toe of the buttress, then climb roughly 9 pitches of steep cracks, slabs, and photogenic gendarme traverse…
Reverse the approach back to the Cascade River Road trailhead.

backups.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams to #3 Camalot (rarely need the #3) with doubles in 0.5, 0.75, and 1 inch, plus a set of nuts; natural gear anchors are used throughout — no fixed anchors on route except the rappel station near the summit.
what_to_bring: glacier travel and crevasse rescue kit
rock rack to #3 Camalot with doubles 0.5-1"
camp gear for the high camp
pro_tips: The summit rappel anchor is a sling around a large boulder about 10m north of the true summit — easy to miss in flat light
The approach gully often holds snow well into summer; crampons make quick work of it on firm morning snow

Pitch 1 trends right about 55-57m (5.6, one 5.7/5.8 move) to a cam anchor; higher up, the cleanest line follows a left-leaning, right-facing corner with good cracks for roughly 90m before blockier terrain leads to the summit ridge.
watch_out: loose blocks in a few spots high on the buttress
steep snow in the approach gully
route-finding through the gendarmes near the top
backups.pro_needs: Good crack systems take cams well throughout; doubles in the 0.5-1" range cover most placements.
backups.best_season: Late July through August, based on typical trip-report dates; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps with the glacier travel but requires crampons on the gully.
backups.approach: The hike-in to the Southwest Buttress follows the identical trailhead-to-glacier approach as the East Ridge: from the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River/Eldorado Creek near the parking area (backtrack downstream to find a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest (no water on this stretch) to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback up past 6,000 ft, and drop via a short Class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin (6,100-6,400 ft, reliable water, a good lower camp/bail-out point). From the basin, ascend 20-30-degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier at about 7,500 ft - rope up for crevasse hazard from here on - and establish a high camp on rock/moraine near the glacier shoulder for the multi-day stay. Where the Southwest Buttress approach diverges is the final glacier traverse: from camp, continue across the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister Glacier, heading toward the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The base of the Southwest Buttress is reached via a prominent gully - often snow-filled year-round - that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side. The recorded round-trip distance is about 25.75 km, somewhat longer than the East Ridge approach because the SW start point is farther along the glacier traverse.
backups.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to a large rock/boulder on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, where a fixed rappel ring and sling (recently reported as reinforced with an additional sling) anchors the route's single rappel: a double-rope rappel (both strands, ~60m rope) that lowers you to a steep snow slope which, in normal-season conditions, keeps a solid connection to the rock, so a moat crossing usually isn't required at this point. From the bottom of that rappel, downclimb/glissade the snow slope to the notch at the base of the route - the same notch used on the approach - and reverse the glacier travel back toward camp. Some parties describe an alternate single-rope-length rappel off the top of the summit gully instead of the ridge-boulder station; functionally this is still a one-rappel descent, just from a slightly different anchor. Either way, plan on exactly one rope-length transition, not a multi-pitch rappel sequence - the rest of the descent is downclimbing, scrambling, and glacier travel. Because this is a moderate Grade III+ route rather than a big-wall-style descent, no v-thread or chained-rappel sequence is needed in summer conditions; the main descent hazard is the moat at the base of the route staying open or widening late in the season, which can complicate reconnecting with the glacier.
backups.bail: Multiple fixed rappel anchors exist along the buttress and near the summit ridge; retreat is generally feasible by rappelling the line of ascent or reversing to the gully.

pitch_detail.notes: A full rope-length up a corner then slightly right; mostly 5.6 climbing with one committing 5.7/5.8 move near the top. Build the anchor on gear (cams to 3 inches) in a crack.
Continue up and right to a small plateau; the belay is built on 0.5-1 inch cams or a few nut placements.
A short class-4 gully scramble gives way to a rising traverse up and left to a comfortable ledge; belay on 1-2 inch cam and nut placements.
A half-rope-length pitch trending left to gain the ridge crest — staying left is important, since climbing right leads into an unwanted 5.10 overhang.

The route's variation crux: a sustained corner past sections of loose rock with limited protection, per multiple trip reports. The standard (non-variation) line instead follows easier low-5th-class ridge scrambling to the same flat shelf.
Climb a right-leaning crack, then continue straight up a wall on good holds; belay off gear near the top of the ridge.
Follow the ridge crest, then traverse left to a wide crack between slabs; the belay is a sling backed up in a notch.
Choose between a loose gully with a chockstone or a rightward line up the wall toward the summit-ridge crack; both options top out near the same point below the final ridge.
A short final traverse along the summit ridge — the same terrain shared with the upper Northwest Ridge — leads to the narrow, exposed high point.

days.note: Same Eldorado Creek trail approach, continuing over talus and the Eldorado Glacier toward the Inspiration/McAllister Glacier area, camping within striking distance of the snow gully below the Marble Creek-McAllister col that gives access to the buttress.
days.title: Approach to high camp near the McAllister/Marble Creek col

days.note: Cross the glacier to the snow-filled gully below the col, gain the blocky toe of the buttress, then climb roughly 9 pitches of steep cracks, slabs, and photogenic gendarme traverses (5.7-5.8) to the summit. Descend by rappelling the approach gully, or via a fixed ring/sling on a boulder near the true summit, then reverse the glacier to camp.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Paved for ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel the rest of the way; the Eldorado Creek trailhead is at about mile 20 and the road continues to the Cascade Pass trailhead. NPS listed the road as open on its road-conditions page as of 3 July 2026 and no longer lists the June 2026 vehicle closure at Eldorado Creek. Washouts and landslides have closed this road at Eldorado Creek repeatedly over the years, so check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
road.driveNote: Not suitable for low-clearance vehicles beyond the pavement; vehicles/trailers over 22 ft or 8 ft wide prohibited beyond mile 18.
road.seasonalGate: Typically snow-gated in winter/spring; usually opens to Cascade Pass trailhead by late June in a normal year.

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows; early snow can arrive by October.
climate.spring: Deep, often unstable snowpack; high avalanche hazard and difficult glacier travel into June.
climate.summer: Primary climbing season, July-September; summer heat can accelerate snowmelt and hazardous stream/moat crossings.
climate.winter: Heavy snowfall, closed access road, avalanche terrain.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: wet, snowy winters and drier summers.

emergency.notes: Cell service is essentially nonexistent from the trailhead into the alpine; carry a satellite communicator.

emergency.sheriffDispatch: Skagit County Sheriff dispatch (360) 336-9450 (after-hours SAR); 911 in an emergency.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, when the glaciers are still well bridged and the buttress rock is dry and snow-free

July.reason: Glacier bridges on the Inspiration and McAllister are strong and the snow-filled approach gully is firm, though ledges on the buttress can still be wet early.

June.reason: Deep snow covers the Eldorado talus and glaciers, which speeds travel, but the buttress ledges still hold snow and the approach slopes carry avalanche risk.

August.reason: Rock on the buttress is dry and the approach gully usually still holds firm snow for crampons, making the glacier crossing and the climb both straightforward.

October.reason: Early snow on the knife-edge summit ridge, short days, and icy glaciers; the Marblemount wilderness office closes mid-October.

September.reason: Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers open wide and the gully can turn icy or loose, adding time to a long approach.

gaps: pitch count varies between sources (9 per Mountain Project vs 12-13 per Mountaineers/SummitPost, likely a difference in how sections are split)
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

rappel_detail.notes: The one rappel: double-rope, onto the steep snow slope that normally still connects to the rock, so no moat crossing is needed here. Then downclimb or glissade the snow to the notch at the base of the route.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed rappel ring and sling on a large boulder (reported reinforced with an extra sling)
hazards: Late in the season the snow can pull away from the rock; check the landing before committing.
rappel_detail.station: A large boulder on the ridge about 10 m north of the true summit, reached by a short downclimb.

backups.rappel_count_note: One double-rope rappel from the fixed ring north of the summit. The alternative is a single-rope rappel from the head of the approach gully, where an open moat at the bottom may need downclimbing or working around.

approach_variants.name: Marble Creek-McAllister pass, then 700 ft down to the snow gully at the toe
approach_variants.notes:
The hike in matches the East Ridge of Eldorado exactly: from the Eldorado trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the river near the parking area (backtrack downstream for a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — no water on this stretch — to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback past 6,000 ft, and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, which has reliable water and is a good lower camp or bail-out point.

From the basin, ascend 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft — rope up from here on — and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

Where this route diverges is the final glacier traverse: cross the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister, heading for the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass, generally crossing on the pass's east side. The base is then reached by a prominent gully, often snow-filled year round, that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
approach_variants.season: Late July through August; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps the glacier travel but wants crampons on the gully
hazards: A steep, often snow-filled approach gully to about 35 degrees
A moat guarding the base of the climb that can present an exposed, deep gap
Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers en route
Loose blocks in places on the upper buttress and unreliable holds described as traps
A large boulder balanced on an overhang ledge near the route
An exposed knife-edge summit ridge at the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the toe of the buttress at the foot of a prominent, often year-round snow gully, and the gully is located by descending — it starts about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass. If you have not lost roughly 700 ft from the pass, you are not at the gully yet.

At the top of that gully there is a fork, and it is the one thing on this peak most worth getting right. This route goes around to the right. The Direct Southwest Buttress instead goes straight up from the same point to three vertical cracks. Same gully, two routes, one turn.

The strongest negative test is published as a warning and it is worth carrying verbatim: do not climb directly below the ridge crest at the start. That variation leads into unwanted 5.10 overhanging terrain on loose rock. If the ground turns overhanging at 5.10 low on the route, you are on the wrong side of the crest and should reverse rather than push on — this route's own crux is 5.8 in a corner and it comes at pitch five, not at the start.

Confirm on pitch one: it is a full rope length, 55 to 57 m, up a corner and then slightly right, mostly 5.6 with one committing 5.7 or 5.8 move near the top, and the anchor is on cams to three inches in a crack. A short first pitch is not this route.

And confirm by which col you crossed: this line is reached over the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The Northwest Ridge starts from a small col at the top of the McAllister's apron on the other side of the Needle and is only three short pitches; the East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a different cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties
